article: Afrofuturism is older than its name. The term itself was coined in 1993 by the cultural critic Mark Dery, but the thing he was naming — Black artists imagining futures, outer space and advanced technology on their own terms — reaches back decades earlier, most famously to the bandleader Sun Ra, who from the 1950s on performed in elaborate Egyptian-and-space-age costuming while claiming (at least as performance, maybe as belief) to be from Saturn. The visual language that developed across jazz, funk and literary science fiction fuses two sources that mainstream science fiction had almost never put together: African and African-diasporic textile, adornment and historical iconography on one hand, and the chrome-and-circuitry vocabulary of space-age technology on the other. The palette that results tends toward deep, saturated jewel tones — purples, golds, deep blues — set against metallic accents, a deliberate departure from science fiction's more common sterile white-and-grey futurism. The look reached its widest audience with the 2018 film Black Panther, whose costume and production design translated decades of Afrofuturist visual thinking into a single, globally seen reference point, and the aesthetic has only grown more visible in fashion and design since.
